name: Sea ice
notes: Frozen sea surface: no plants; near-empty is correct. Only ice-algae (diatoms) colour the underside of the floes, and polar ice-edge rock carries crustose lichen and moss where floes ground against shore (Arctic and Antarctic).

ground.name: Antarctic moss
ground.source: Bryum pseudotriquetrum, bipolar moss of polar coastal rock and meltwater seeps beside sea ice, cushions 1-5 cm — Wikipedia / British Antarctic Survey

traits.native_range: Bryum pseudotriquetrum, bipolar moss of polar coastal rock and meltwater seeps beside sea ice, cushions 1-5 cm — Wikiped
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

ground.silhouette: low green moss cushion with red-brown stems

growth.juvenile_note: Spores or shoot fragments sprout into green protonema threads on wet gravel or seepage mud; small upright shoots with lance-shaped, red-based leaves and a strong midrib appear within weeks, then crowd into a dense turf, green above and wine-red to brown below, bound together by reddish rhizoid felt.
growth.source: Cosmopolitan moss of fens, seepages and streamsides and one of the commonest Antarctic mosses, where sporophytes are rare and shoots extend only a few mm a year; timings estimated from moss growth studies.

ground.name: Ice algae
ground.source: underwater — Nitzschia frigida, dominant Arctic sea-ice diatom, brown algal film on the underside of floes, mm-cm scale — Wikipedia / polar research literature

traits.native_range: underwater — Nitzschia frigida, dominant Arctic sea-ice diatom, brown algal film on the underside of floes, mm-cm scale
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

ground.silhouette: brown stain film on the underside of sea ice

growth.juvenile_note: No juvenile form: single glassy, boat-shaped diatom cells divide every few days and link into ribbon- or tree-like colonies in the brine channels at the underside of sea ice. By spring they stain the bottom few centimetres of the ice golden-brown, then are released into the water as the ice melts; a few cells overwinter in the ice to seed next year's bloom.
growth.source: Arctic sea-ice algae literature (N. frigida is the key colonial pennate diatom of bottom-ice communities; spring bloom roughly Mar-Jun when light returns, growth at <1% of surface light, released at ice melt); values are for the visible bloom layer

ground.name: Map lichen
ground.source: Rhizocarpon geographicum, Arctic and Antarctic ice-edge rock and nunataks, yellow-green crustose lichen, mm-thick — Wikipedia

traits.native_range: Rhizocarpon geographicum, Arctic and Antarctic ice-edge rock and nunataks, yellow-green crustose lichen, mm-thick — Wiki
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

ground.silhouette: yellow-green crust map with black borders on rock

growth.juvenile_note: Begins as a thin black stain (prothallus) on bare, sunlit siliceous rock. Tiny angular chartreuse-yellow areoles (0.2-1.8 mm) appear on it like islands and multiply into a flat crust split by black lines, like a map; neighbouring thalli meet along black borders. Small black fruit bodies sit between the areoles. It widens by well under 1 mm a year.
growth.source: Wikipedia Rhizocarpon geographicum (patches to ~15 cm; areoles 0.2-1.8 mm; black apothecia under 1.5 mm; age estimates 9,500 yr on Baffin Island and 10,000-11,500 yr in the Brooks Range; used in lichenometry); diameter growth of roughly 0.1-1 mm/yr from lichenometry studies (knowledge)
